title: AI in Education #3: Five Things I Learned from Adam Boxer
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton distills five takeaways from a conversation with Adam Boxer, a science teacher at The Totteridge Academy and co-creator of Carousel Learning, who is more sceptical about AI in education than most guests in the series. Boxer opposes any student-facing AI tool at present because students reliably take the path of least resistance, and once they are told it is acceptable to use AI 'responsibly' the seal is broken and they will use it uncontrolled elsewhere -- echoing Michael Pershan's line that any tutor the tutee can control is not a tutor. He is more open to AI in marking, but argues the value lies in AI handling bulk tick-cross work and generating a report the teacher is obliged to act on, not in replacing the teacher's engagement with the work. His sharpest warning concerns resource creation: AI may raise the floor for weak teachers but could hollow out the intellectual labour -- writing thousands of questions -- that built expert teachers like himself, and he doubts most teachers will use AI as a genuine thought partner rather than a shortcut. He sees promise but real danger in AI-based lesson-transcript coaching, since a transcript misses most of what happens in a room and can misapply research like Rosenshine's principles. His overall prediction, delivered with characteristic bluntness, is that AI will not revolutionise education because no ed-tech ever has -- schools change slowly, and the gap between LinkedIn hype and classroom reality remains enormous.
points: Boxer opposes student-facing AI outright because students take the path of least resistance, and permitting 'responsible' use breaks the seal so they treat AI as acceptable everywhere, not just in the constrained tool a school sanctions.

The productive use of AI in marking is not replacing teacher judgment but offloading the mechanical tick-cross work into a report the teacher is obliged to review and act on, preserving the professional engagement that spotting trends requires.

AI-generated resources could eliminate the worst teaching (a genuine gain) while hollowing out the intellectual labour -- writing thousands of questions over years -- that produces the best teachers, since most teachers will default to a single lazy prompt rather than iterative refinement.

AI lesson-transcript coaching can usefully flag wait time and questioning patterns a human observer misses in real time, but a transcript cannot see physicality or tone, and training data 'worse than trash' risks pushing teachers toward debunked practices like learning styles.

Boxer's prediction is that AI will not revolutionise education because nothing ever has -- Encarta, Google, Wikipedia, and interactive whiteboards were all supposed to transform classrooms and did not, because schools change like tankers, not speedboats.
quotes: You need to communicate to students that using AI is dumb and it is a waste of their time and will rot their brain.
any tutor that the tutee can control is not a tutor. The moment you open a chat interface, the student becomes the agent.

You have been in schools long enough to know that is not how your bottom 50% of teachers are going to be using it. They are going to go, can you give me 10 multiple-choice questions about Pythagoras, and that is what they are going to use.
He put it to me bluntly: “You would not exist.” And he is right. I have written God knows how many multiple-choice diagnostic questions.
AI is not going to revolutionise education. It is not going to happen. And what is the proof of this? That nothing ever does.

There is such a big chasm between what people on LinkedIn think will happen in schools and what schools are actually really like. You go to a typical school, and there will still be posters on the wall from ten years ago.
